summary: This standards-track document defines a well-known BGP community called GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN. A router tags routes with it before a planned session shutdown so neighbors can prefer alternative paths first. It also describes operational procedures so that traffic moves away before the session goes down, reducing lost traffic during planned maintenance.

eli5.summary: Before closing a road for repairs, you put up a sign telling drivers to use another route. This is that sign for internet routers, so nobody drives into a closed road.

subtitle: A well-known BGP community that tells neighbors to move traffic away before a planned session shutdown.

tldr.problem: Shutting down an EBGP session for planned maintenance can cause packet loss while BGP converges, because some routers briefly have no path to affected prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: Before shutdown, the initiator tags routes with the GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN community and receivers lower their LOCAL_PREF, so alternate paths are chosen while the old path stays usable until they are ready.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that renamed the existing planned-shut community (0xFFFF0000) to GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN and gives operators a standard way to drain a session.

today: RFC 8326 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Planned Maintenance Without Packet Loss
sections.content:
Routing changes in BGP can be caused by planned maintenance. This document defines a well-known community (RFC 1997) called GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN to cut the management overhead of gracefully shutting down BGP sessions. Implementers can use it to build an automated mechanism that needs no router reconfiguration at maintenance time.

The procedures target loss caused by the BGP convergence that follows shutting down an EBGP session between two Autonomous System Border Routers (ASBRs). They apply when the forwarding plane is affected, so Graceful Restart does not apply. The goal is to meet the requirements of RFC 6198 as well as possible without changing BGP. Shutting down an IBGP session and establishing an EBGP session are out of scope.
sections.eli5: When a router is about to go offline for a planned fix, it should warn its neighbors first so they can pick another route without anyone losing messages.

sections.title: Why Packets Are Lost
sections.content:
The RFC names two reasons for packet loss after a manual EBGP shutdown. First, some routers may have no path to an affected prefix, because alternate paths can be hidden. That happens when the extension of RFC 7911 is not used and the alternate paths are not selected as best by the ASBRs that receive them, or Route Reflectors do not propagate them because they did not select them as best.

Second, the FIB can be inconsistent between routers in the AS, so packets can loop and be dropped unless encapsulation is used inside the AS. This document only addresses the first reason.
sections.eli5: If a road is closed before anyone has learned the detour, cars have nowhere to go. The detour must be known before the closure.

sections.title: The Graceful Shutdown Procedure
sections.content:
The idea is to keep the paths being shut down, but with a lower LOCAL_PREF, instead of simply withdrawing them. The old paths stay usable while alternates are selected and propagated. The value SHOULD be lower than any alternative path, and the RECOMMENDED value is 0.

Pre-configuration. On each ASBR that supports the receiver role, an inbound policy on all EBGP sessions matches the GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN community and sets LOCAL_PREF of tagged paths to a low value.

At maintenance time the operator on the initiator:

  • applies an outbound policy that tags paths sent over the session with the community, which triggers re-advertisement of all active routes;
  • applies an inbound policy that tags received paths with the community and sets a low LOCAL_PREF;
  • waits for re-advertisement and BGP convergence on both ASBRs;
  • shuts down the session, optionally using RFC 8203 to communicate the reason.

To shut down a whole router, routes the router originates, such as aggregates or static routes redistributed into BGP, are also tagged with the community and given a low LOCAL_PREF.
sections.eli5: First everyone agrees that anything marked with the sign counts as the worst choice. Then the closing router puts the sign on its roads, waits until everybody has switched, and only then locks the gate.

sections.title: Implementation and IANA Notes
sections.content:
BGP implementers SHOULD provide configuration knobs that use the GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN community to inform neighbors about an impending shutdown. How to implement them is outside the scope. The appendix gives non-normative policy examples for Cisco IOS XR, BIRD and OpenBGPD that match the community and set the local preference to 0.

IANA had previously assigned the value 0xFFFF0000 to a community named planned-shut in the BGP Well-known Communities registry. IANA renamed it to GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN and pointed the reference at this document.
sections.eli5: Router makers should add a simple button for sending the warning. The sign already had a number, and it just got a clearer name.

sections.title: Rejected Alternatives and Related Cases
sections.content:
Two alternatives were considered but rejected for limited applicability. Raising the Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED) of the paths to avoid only works if the alternate paths are as good with respect to LOCAL_PREF and AS path length. Increasing the IGP distance to the BGP NEXT_HOP only works if alternates are also as good in LOCAL_PREF, AS path length and MED, and it cannot be used with BGP NEXT_HOP self.

The appendix also notes that for an IBGP session shutdown, if the IBGP topology stays viable afterwards, no specific graceful shutdown action is needed. It discusses transient losses when establishing an EBGP session, and says RFC 7911 or best-external advertisement can help in some corner cases.
sections.eli5: Other tricks, like making a road look a bit longer, only work when the detour is just as good. The LOCAL_PREF sign works more broadly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
By offering graceful shutdown to a neighboring AS, an ISP gives that neighbor, and possibly its downstream ASes, a way to lower the LOCAL_PREF of the paths the ISP receives from them.

The neighbor could abuse this for inbound traffic engineering, declaring that some prefixes are under maintenance to push traffic to another peering link. If the ISP does not tolerate that, it SHOULD monitor the use of the community.
sections.eli5: Someone could put up a fake road-closed sign just to send cars down their favorite street. The road owner should watch for that.

messages.label: Re-advertise routes with GRACEFUL_SHUTDOWN
messages.note: Outbound policy tags every active route.

messages.label: Re-advertise routes (tagged by receiver policy)
messages.note: The receiver's inbound policy lowers LOCAL_PREF; both sides converge.

messages.label: Shut down EBGP session
messages.note: Optionally with the reason from RFC 8203.
